details:
**Hungarian Rhapsodies**
Liszt's set of 19 virtuosic piano pieces based on Roma ("Gypsy") music and verbunkos dance tunes from his native Hungary. Many alternate a slow, brooding lassan section with a fast, wild friska, use the "Gypsy" scale, and imitate the cimbalom, a hammered dulcimer. No. 2 is the most famous, and No. 15 is based on the "Rákóczi March."

**Transcendental Etudes**
A set of 12 extremely difficult piano studies, grown out of a set of studies Liszt wrote at age fifteen, and dedicated to his teacher Carl Czerny. They include No. 4, "Mazeppa," which depicts a Cossack tied to a galloping horse (Liszt also wrote a symphonic poem of the same name), and No. 5, "Feux follets" ("Will-o'-the-wisps").

**Mephisto Waltzes**
Four waltzes inspired by Nikolaus Lenau's version of Faust, not Goethe's. The first, "The Dance in the Village Inn," opens with stacked fifths in 3/8 time that imitate Mephistopheles tuning a violin he has grabbed from a fiddler, before he plays wild music while Faust dances. The late "Bagatelle without Tonality" was labeled as a fourth Mephisto Waltz.

**"La Campanella"**
The third of Liszt's six Grandes études de Paganini, based on the rondo of Paganini's Violin Concerto No. 2. The right hand jumps rapidly between the melody and a high, repeated D-sharp that represents the little bell of the title.

**Lisztomania**
The term Heinrich Heine used for the frenzied fan hysteria, especially among women, at Liszt's concerts in the 1840s. Liszt is also credited with inventing the modern solo recital, playing from memory with the piano turned sideways to the audience.

**Symphonic poem and Les Préludes**
Liszt coined the term "symphonic poem" for a one-movement orchestral work that tells a story or illustrates a program, and he wrote 13 of them, including Prometheus, Orpheus, and Mazeppa. The most famous, Les Préludes, takes its title from an ode by Alphonse de Lamartine and grows out of a short three-note motif.

**Years of Pilgrimage (Années de pèlerinage)**
Three piano suites inspired by Liszt's travels. "First Year: Switzerland" includes "William Tell's Chapel" and "Au bord d'une source" ("Beside a Spring"). "Second Year: Italy" includes the Petrarch Sonnets, "Il penseroso" (after a Michelangelo statue), and the Dante Sonata, with the supplement "Venice and Naples" (Gondoliera, Canzone, Tarantella). "Third Year" includes the threnodies "To the Cypresses of the Villa d'Este."

**Dante Sonata**
"Après une lecture du Dante: Fantasia quasi sonata," a one-movement piece in Years of Pilgrimage whose title comes from a Victor Hugo poem. It opens with octaves on A and E-flat, separated by the dissonant tritone, to depict the gates of Hell.

**Liebesträume**
"Dreams of Love," three piano nocturnes based on poems by Ludwig Uhland and Ferdinand Freiligrath. The third, in A-flat, sets Freiligrath's "O lieb, so lang du lieben kannst" ("Love as long as you can"), and its sections are separated by difficult cadenzas.

**Totentanz**
"Dance of Death," a piece for piano and orchestra made of variations on the medieval "Dies irae" chant, the same melody Berlioz used in the Symphonie fantastique. It opens with harsh, percussive piano writing and is full of glissandi.

**Faust Symphony**
Liszt's three-movement symphony based on Goethe's Faust, with one movement each for Faust, Gretchen, and Mephistopheles. His Dante Symphony is a similar program symphony based on the Divine Comedy.

**Piano Sonata in B minor**
Liszt's massive one-movement sonata, which develops a few themes throughout the whole piece. He dedicated it to Robert Schumann.

**Don Sanche**
Liszt's only opera, written when he was a teenager. In it, the magician Alidor, lord of the Castle of Love, tests Princess Elzire's love for Don Sanche. The manuscript was lost for decades.

**Weimar and the New German School**
As music director at Weimar, Liszt led the progressive "New German School" against the conservatives (Brahms's camp) in the War of the Romantics. He conducted the 1850 premiere of Wagner's Lohengrin, and Wagner later married Liszt's daughter Cosima.

**Transcriptions, paraphrases, and the Hexameron**
Liszt made piano transcriptions of all nine Beethoven symphonies and opera "paraphrases," such as one on the Rigoletto quartet. He also wrote the introduction to the collaborative Hexameron variations on the "March of the Puritans," which is tied to his famous piano "duel" with Sigismond Thalberg at Princess Belgiojoso's salon.
